content:
Apple has cited a recently paused securities fraud lawsuit to support its request to halt further proceedings in a lower court while the Supreme Court reviews parts of its legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Apple invoked the ruling to help Judge Rogers decide whether to pause the case.

Earlier this year, a class action filed on behalf of the Coral Springs Police Officers Pension Plan accused Apple of securities fraud.

The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled investors into believing the company was in compliance with the injunction in the Epic Games case and on track to deliver its announced AI Siri features.

Meanwhile, Apple continues to challenge a finding of civil contempt in the Epic case. The Supreme Court is weighing an issue: the 2021 injunction required Apple to allow external payment options but did not explicitly bar it from collecting commissions on such transactions; the Supreme Court must decide whether Apple can be held in civil contempt for charging commissions on transactions made outside the App Store.

Last week, Apple asked the lower court to pause proceedings to determine what commissions, if any, the company can collect on transactions outside the App Store while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt finding.

Apple argued the Supreme Court's ruling will affect the lower court proceedings, but Epic Games disputes this characterization.

In fact, Apple had filed a similar request to pause proceedings in the Coral Springs securities fraud case because it too involves the Epic Games case.

Earlier today, Judge Noël Wise granted Apple's request, meaning the Coral Springs case will remain paused until the Supreme Court rules on the civil contempt finding.

This ruling prompted Apple to submit Judge Wise's decision in the Epic Games matter to Judge Rogers to argue that its request for Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to pause proceedings should likewise be granted.

Excerpt from Apple's filing to Judge Rogers:

Judge Rogers is now weighing Apple's arguments in favor of pausing the case and Epic's arguments against doing so. Apple is hoping Judge Wise's decision will persuade Judge Rogers to reach the same conclusion.

Notably, in its reply regarding Epic's opposition to pausing the case, Apple also asked Judge Gonzalez Rogers to, if she denies the request to pause, hold proceedings in abeyance so the company can seek to keep the case frozen from the Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court while the high court separately reviews the contempt ruling.
